desc:
Each index of nums is chosen independently with probability one half, so every one of the 2n subsets of indices is equally likely (the empty subset included). Find the probability that the bitwise XOR of the chosen values equals target.

Return it as a reduced fraction p/q with no spaces. Remember that the XOR of an empty subset is 0.

nums = [1, 2, 3], target = 0 -> 1/4
nums = [1, 2, 3], target = 4 -> 0/1
nums = [5], target = 5       -> 1/2
nums = [], target = 0        -> 1/1
hints: Gaussian elimination over GF(2) works for XOR. Build a basis of the values: keep at most one value per leading bit. Let r be the number of basis vectors.
Every value in the span of the basis is produced by exactly 2n - r of the subsets, and values outside the span by none. So the probability is 2-r when the target is in the span.
To test membership, reduce the target by the basis from the highest bit down. The target is in the span exactly when it reduces to 0.
editorial: Look at the linear map from subsets to XOR values. Think of each value as a vector over GF(2). The set of all XORs of subsets is the span of the vectors, and a basis of the span has r vectors. Gaussian elimination builds such a basis in O(n * 30) time: insert each value by clearing its highest set bit with an existing basis vector, or store it as a new basis vector under that bit.

Fix a target t in the span. Choose the subsets' membership for all indices except a set of r pivot indices freely; the pivot choices are then forced, so exactly 2n - r subsets give XOR t. Dividing by the 2n total gives 1 / 2r. If t is outside the span, no subset works and the answer is 0/1.

The membership test reduces t from the highest bit down: whenever bit b is set and there is a basis vector with leading bit b, XOR it in. If the result is 0 the target is in the span. The empty subset makes 0 always reachable, so the answer for target 0 is 1 / 2r.
